cards.q: Membrane structure: lipid matrix and what it limits
cards.a: Phospholipid + cholesterol bilayer; nonpolar core gives high resistance and impermeability

cards.q: Main route for most drugs across membranes
cards.a: Passive diffusion, down the concentration gradient; membrane plays no active role

cards.q: Rate of passive diffusion depends on
cards.a: Lipid:water partition coefficient of the drug

cards.q: Factor that slows diffusion (Fick's law)
cards.a: Greater membrane thickness

cards.q: Passive diffusion rate increases with
cards.a: Concentration, membrane area and permeability coefficient

cards.q: Why the body has few transporters for drugs
cards.a: Drugs are xenobiotics; transporters exist mainly for normal metabolites

cards.q: Facilitated diffusion: energy needed?
cards.a: No; moves solute down its electrochemical gradient

cards.q: Carrier superfamily for facilitated diffusion
cards.a: Solute carrier (SLC) transporters

cards.q: Example of facilitated diffusion
cards.a: Glucose entry into muscle and fat via GLUT4

cards.q: Primary active transport energy source
cards.a: Direct hydrolysis of ATP

cards.q: Primary active transporter superfamily
cards.a: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters

cards.q: Direction ABC transporters move solutes
cards.a: Efflux only: out of cytoplasm to outside or into organelles

cards.q: Secondary active transport: energy comes from
cards.a: Downhill movement of another solute, usually Na+

cards.q: Symport versus antiport
cards.a: Symport: both solutes same direction. Antiport: opposite directions (exchange)

cards.q: Drugs using normal-metabolite transporters: example
cards.a: Levodopa and methyldopa absorbed by the aromatic amino acid transporter

cards.q: Carrier-mediated transport kinetics
cards.a: Saturable, Michaelis-Menten, specific, competitively inhibited, slower than channels

cards.q: What sets the maximum rate (Vmax) of carrier transport
cards.a: Density of the transporter in the membrane

cards.q: What Km of a carrier represents
cards.a: Substrate concentration giving half-maximal transport; reflects affinity

cards.q: Effect of genetic polymorphism on transporters
cards.a: Alters transporter density and affinity, so changes drug PK

cards.q: Tissue-specific drug distribution is due to
cards.a: Transporters present only in certain cells

cards.q: Vesicular transport: which substances mainly
cards.a: Proteins and very large molecules; contributes little to most drugs

cards.q: Vitamin B12 absorption mechanism
cards.a: Binds intrinsic factor; absorbed as that complex

cards.q: Hormones and noradrenaline are released by
cards.a: Exocytosis from storage vesicles

cards.q: Passage through aqueous pores: size limit in most cells
cards.a: Pores about 4 Angstrom; MW above about 100-200 cannot pass

cards.q: Capillary paracellular spaces (except brain)
cards.a: About 40 Angstrom; most drugs, even albumin, filter through

cards.q: What governs drug transfer across capillaries
cards.a: Blood flow rate, not lipid solubility or pH

cards.q: Are nonelectrolytes such as ethanol pH-dependent on transport?
cards.a: No; transport is pH independent

cards.q: Filtration: which drugs pass through pores
cards.a: Lipid-insoluble drugs smaller than the pore diameter

cards.q: What filtration depends on
cards.a: Pore or paracellular size, and hydrodynamic flow under pressure

cards.q: pH at which a weak drug is 50% ionised
cards.a: Its pKa

cards.q: Henderson equation for a weak acid
cards.a: pH = pKa + log [A-]/[HA]

cards.q: Effect of a 1-unit pH change on ionised:unionised ratio
cards.a: Tenfold change

cards.q: Weak acids form salts with
cards.a: Cations (e.g. sodium phenobarbitone); ionise more at alkaline pH

cards.q: Weak bases form salts with
cards.a: Anions (e.g. atropine sulfate, chloroquine phosphate); ionise more at acid pH

cards.q: Ion trapping definition
cards.a: Weak electrolyte ionises on the far side and cannot escape, so accumulates

cards.q: Drug mainly absorbed from the stomach: weak acid example
cards.a: Aspirin (pKa 3.5), unionised at gastric pH

cards.q: Weak bases: where are they mainly absorbed
cards.a: Intestine, after reaching it (ionised in stomach), e.g. morphine, quinine

cards.q: Aspirin mucosal damage mechanism
cards.a: Ion trapping in gastric mucosal cells at pH 7.0

cards.q: Why basic drugs reach higher intracellular concentration
cards.a: Intracellular pH 7.0 versus plasma 7.4

cards.q: Acidic drugs excretion in alkaline urine
cards.a: Stay ionised, do not back-diffuse in tubules, excreted faster

cards.q: Basic drugs are excreted faster when urine is
cards.a: Acidified

cards.q: Range of urine pH in kidney tubules
cards.a: About 4.5 to 8

cards.q: Sodium bicarbonate promotes excretion of
cards.a: Weak acids such as aspirin and urate

cards.q: Why second-generation H1 antihistamines cause little sedation
cards.a: Ionised and less lipophilic, so they poorly cross the BBB (loratadine)

cards.q: Strong acids and strong bases: effect of media pH
cards.a: Always ionised; pH does not change their ionisation

cards.q: Aspirin (pKa 3.5) percent unionised at pH 2.5
cards.a: About 90% unionised, 10% ionised

cards.q: Aspirin (pKa 3.5) percent unionised at pH 1.5
cards.a: About 99% unionised, 1% ionised

cards.q: Morphine absorbed from stomach and small intestine
cards.a: About 1% stomach, 99% small intestine

cards.q: Aspirin absorbed from stomach and small intestine
cards.a: About 10% stomach, 90% small intestine

cards.q: Effect of antacids on acidic drug absorption
cards.a: Reduce stomach absorption of acidic drugs by neutralising HCl

cards.q: Why most drugs absorb from the small intestine despite pH
cards.a: Very large surface area of villi (about 200 m2)

cards.q: Stomach: surface area and mucus effect on absorption
cards.a: Small surface area and a mucus layer slow absorption even of acidic drugs

cards.q: Typical pH: stomach versus upper intestine
cards.a: Stomach about 1-2; upper intestine about 3-6

cards.q: Gene encoding P-glycoprotein
cards.a: MDR1 (ABCB1)

cards.q: P-glycoprotein transporter class
cards.a: Primary active ABC efflux transporter (ATP-driven)

cards.q: P-glycoprotein locations: list all
cards.a: Intestinal mucosa, renal tubules, bile canaliculi, choroid plexus, astrocyte foot processes (BBB), testicular and placental microvessels

cards.q: P-glycoprotein effect on oral absorption
cards.a: Pumps drug back into the gut lumen, limiting absorption

cards.q: P-glycoprotein effect on brain, testes and foetus
cards.a: Limits entry of drugs into them

cards.q: P-glycoprotein effect on elimination
cards.a: Promotes biliary and renal elimination

cards.q: Other primary active transporters of pharmacological importance
cards.a: MRP2 and BCRP

cards.q: P-gp inhibition effect on digoxin
cards.a: Raises digoxin oral bioavailability; toxicity risk

cards.q: P-glycoprotein inhibitors: list
cards.a: Quinidine, verapamil, amiodarone, cyclosporin, ketoconazole, erythromycin or clarithromycin, ritonavir (QVACKER)

cards.q: P-glycoprotein inducers: examples
cards.a: Rifampicin and phenobarbitone; they lower oral bioavailability of P-gp substrates

cards.q: Cyclosporin effect on bile secretion via P-gp
cards.a: Reduces biliary secretion, causing bile accumulation and cholestatic jaundice

cards.q: Verapamil role in cancer chemotherapy
cards.a: Blocks P-gp, reversing drug resistance in cancer cells

cards.q: Why digoxin oral bioavailability is low
cards.a: Partly P-gp efflux from gut epithelium back into the lumen

cards.q: Other drug with low oral bioavailability from P-gp efflux
cards.a: Cyclosporine

cards.q: Effect of P-gp inducers on digoxin urinary excretion
cards.a: Increased urinary excretion, reducing digoxin effect

cards.q: Efflux transporters at placenta: examples
cards.a: P-gp, BCRP and MRP3 limit foetal exposure

cards.q: Bioavailability definition
cards.a: Fraction of administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged

cards.q: Bioavailability formula
cards.a: F = quantity reaching systemic circulation / quantity administered

cards.q: Bioavailability of IV dose
cards.a: 100% by definition

cards.q: Causes of oral bioavailability below 100%
cards.a: Incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism or biliary excretion

cards.q: Bioavailability is measured from
cards.a: Area under the concentration-time curve or urinary excretion

cards.q: Units of bioavailability
cards.a: None; it is a fraction, F

cards.q: Bioequivalence definition
cards.a: Rate and extent of bioavailability not significantly different under identical test conditions

cards.q: Pharmaceutical equivalence criteria
cards.a: Same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route

cards.q: Acceptable generic bioavailability range (US FDA)
cards.a: 80-125% of the reference product

cards.q: Why chemically equal products may not be bioequivalent
cards.a: Formulation and manufacture change disintegration and dissolution

cards.q: Drugs with low safety margin where brand switching matters: list
cards.a: Digoxin, oral hypoglycaemics, oral anticoagulants

cards.q: Drugs where brands must never be interchanged: list
cards.a: Phenytoin, theophylline, cyclosporin

cards.q: Phenytoin brand interchange: why 80-125% is unacceptable
cards.a: Small rise in absorption causes toxicity; small fall causes rebound seizures

cards.q: Rate of dissolution governed by
cards.a: Inherent solubility, particle size and crystal form

cards.q: Particle size reduction example
cards.a: Microfine aspirin increases its absorption rate

cards.q: Griseofulvin and spironolactone: effect of microfining
cards.a: Amount in tablet can be halved for the same effect

cards.q: Does a freely soluble drug need particle size reduction?
cards.a: No, e.g. paracetamol

cards.q: Ketoconazole absorption requirement
cards.a: Dissolves at low pH; needs gastric acid

cards.q: Factors affecting tablet disintegration
cards.a: Excipients, binders and compression force used in manufacture

cards.q: Enteric coating purpose
cards.a: Prevents dissolution in gastric acid; protects acid-labile drugs and limits irritation

cards.q: Drugs degraded by gastric acid and by peptidases
cards.a: Penicillin G (acid); insulin (peptidases)

cards.q: Effect of food on oral absorption
cards.a: Dilutes drug, delays gastric emptying, may form poorly absorbed complexes

cards.q: Exception where food increases absorption
cards.a: Lumefantrine (fatty food)

cards.q: Tetracycline absorption interaction with milk
cards.a: Forms poorly absorbed complex with calcium

cards.q: Time gap to avoid luminal interactions (tetracyclines, iron, antacids)
cards.a: Give the two drugs 2-3 hours apart

cards.q: Highly ionised drugs given orally
cards.a: Poorly absorbed (e.g. gentamicin, neostigmine)

cards.q: Drugs that slow gut motility: list
cards.a: Anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids

cards.q: Drug that speeds gut motility
cards.a: Metoclopramide

cards.q: Drugs that damage gut mucosa and impair absorption: list
cards.a: Neomycin, methotrexate, vinblastine

cards.q: Antibiotics and gut flora effect on drug disposition
cards.a: Disrupt enterohepatic cycling of oral contraceptives and digoxin

cards.q: Sublingual absorption benefit
cards.a: Venous drainage goes to superior vena cava, bypassing first-pass

cards.q: Why sublingual nitroglycerin acts quickly
cards.a: Nonionic, highly lipid soluble, avoids first-pass

cards.q: Share of rectally absorbed drug that bypasses the liver
cards.a: About 50%

cards.q: Rectal drug draining via internal haemorrhoidal vein goes to
cards.a: Portal vein, so it undergoes first-pass

cards.q: Rectal diazepam: clinical use
cards.a: Drug of choice for febrile seizures in children

cards.q: Drugs with high first-pass metabolism (Prep list)
cards.a: Fentanyl, propranolol, lignocaine, morphine, natural steroids, verapamil, aldosterone, pethidine, cortisol, salbutamol, testosterone, imipramine, progesterone, GTN, estrogen

cards.q: Oral route first-pass: how to avoid it
cards.a: Give by parenteral route, or sublingual or buccal route

cards.q: Why oral bioavailability is lower than IV
cards.a: Drug passes portal vein and liver before systemic circulation

cards.q: Route bioavailability ranges (Prep): IV
cards.a: 100 (by definition)

cards.q: Route bioavailability ranges (Prep): IM and SC
Route bioavailability ranges (Prep): oral and inhalation
cards.a: 5 to less than 100%

cards.q: Route bioavailability ranges (Prep): rectal and transdermal
cards.a: Rectal 30 to less than 100%; transdermal 80 to 100%

cards.q: Transdermal absorption: what determines dose
cards.a: Area of the patch rather than its thickness

cards.q: Transdermal absorption: what determines skin penetration
cards.a: Lipid solubility of the drug and surface area applied

cards.q: Skin absorption enhancement methods
cards.a: Rub drug in oily vehicle; occlusive dressing hydrates skin

cards.q: Drugs that penetrate intact skin significantly: list
cards.a: Hyoscine, fentanyl, GTN, nicotine, testosterone, estradiol

cards.q: Abraded or burned skin absorption
cards.a: Systemic absorption much easier

cards.q: Corticosteroid skin risk over large areas
cards.a: Systemic effects and pituitary-adrenal suppression

cards.q: Organophosphate skin contact risk
cards.a: Systemic toxicity

cards.q: Cornea permeability: physostigmine versus neostigmine
cards.a: Physostigmine (unionised) crosses; neostigmine (ionised) does not

cards.q: Eye drop systemic absorption route
cards.a: Nasolacrimal duct; timolol can cause bradycardia and asthma

cards.q: Vaginal oestrogen cream adverse effect in male partner
cards.a: Gynaecomastia

cards.q: Subcutaneous versus intramuscular absorption speed
cards.a: S.c. slower than i.m.; both faster and more predictable than oral

cards.q: Heat and exercise effect on s.c. or i.m. absorption
cards.a: Accelerate absorption by increasing blood flow

cards.q: Adrenaline in local anaesthetic injection
cards.a: Vasoconstriction slows absorption

cards.q: Hyaluronidase role in injection
cards.a: Promotes spread and speeds absorption from s.c. site

cards.q: Route for very large molecules after s.c. injection
cards.a: Lymphatics

cards.q: Depot preparations: examples
cards.a: Benzathine penicillin, protamine zinc insulin, depot progestins

cards.q: Z-track (zigzag) injection technique purpose
cards.a: Avoids staining of subcutaneous fat by leaking drug (e.g. iron dextran)

cards.q: Inhalation: particle size for local versus systemic action
cards.a: 2-5 micron for local action; under 2 micron reaches alveoli for systemic action

cards.q: Increase AUC in order to raise bioavailability
cards.a: Increase absorption or reduce first-pass metabolism or elimination

cards.q: Bioavailability depends on which two parameters
cards.a: Directly proportional to absorption; inversely proportional to first-pass metabolism

cards.q: Apparent volume of distribution definition
cards.a: Volume that would hold all drug at the plasma concentration

cards.q: Volume of distribution formula
cards.a: Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration

cards.q: Volume of distribution units
cards.a: Litres, or L/kg

cards.q: Vd of lipid-insoluble drugs: approximates what volume
cards.a: Extracellular fluid volume (e.g. streptomycin, gentamicin about 0.25 L/kg)

cards.q: Vd of diclofenac and warfarin (both 99% bound)
cards.a: About 0.15 L/kg, restricted to vascular compartment

cards.q: Digoxin apparent Vd
cards.a: About 6 L/kg (sequestered in tissues)

cards.q: Propranolol and morphine apparent Vd
cards.a: Propranolol 4 L/kg; morphine 3.5 L/kg

cards.q: Meaning of a large Vd
cards.a: Most drug is in extravascular tissue; plasma level is low

cards.q: Factors governing volume of distribution: list
cards.a: Lipid:water partition, pKa, plasma protein binding, tissue affinity, fat:lean mass (age, sex, obesity)

cards.q: Disease states altering Vd: list
cards.a: Congestive heart failure, uraemia, cirrhosis

cards.q: Haemodialysis and drugs with large Vd
cards.a: Not easily removed, since little is in plasma

cards.q: Most important factor reducing Vd (Prep)
cards.a: Increased plasma protein binding

cards.q: Vd of chloroquine (RR5)
cards.a: About 13,000 L, highest of the listed drugs

cards.q: Features of a low-Vd drug
cards.a: Stays in blood, water soluble, ionised, large molecule, highly protein bound

cards.q: Plasma protein that binds acidic drugs
cards.a: Albumin (also the more abundant binder)

cards.q: Plasma protein that binds basic drugs
cards.a: Alpha-1 acid glycoprotein

cards.q: Acidic drugs bound mainly to albumin: list
cards.a: Barbiturates, benzodiazepines, NSAIDs, valproic acid, phenytoin, penicillins, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, tolbutamide, warfarin

cards.q: Basic drugs bound mainly to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein: list
cards.a: Beta-blockers, bupivacaine, lidocaine, disopyramide, imipramine, methadone, prazosin, quinidine, verapamil

cards.q: Bound fraction of a drug is
cards.a: Not available for action; temporary storage in equilibrium with free drug

cards.q: Why highly protein-bound drugs act long
cards.a: Bound fraction is not metabolised or excreted unless actively extracted

cards.q: Renal clearance above total renal blood flow occurs when
cards.a: Active tubular secretion removes free drug, releasing bound drug

cards.q: Penicillin elimination half-life
cards.a: About 30 min, because of active secretion

cards.q: Effect of displacement on plasma drug level
cards.a: Free concentration rises transiently; usually minor unless tissue binding or clearance changes

cards.q: Do probenecid and indomethacin displace each other?
cards.a: No; binding sites do not overlap

cards.q: Do acidic drugs displace basic drugs?
cards.a: Generally not

cards.q: Hypoalbuminaemia effect on phenytoin
cards.a: Free fraction rises, so toxicity risk

cards.q: Uraemia effect on protein binding of phenytoin and pethidine
cards.a: Binding reduced

cards.q: Pregnancy and inflammation effect on propranolol binding
cards.a: Binding increased (alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises)

cards.q: Phenytoin and valproate interaction
cards.a: Valproate displaces phenytoin from albumin, raising free phenytoin

cards.q: Which concentration is quoted for drug plasma levels
cards.a: Total drug, bound and free; compare free drug for MIC

cards.q: S-warfarin versus R-warfarin volume
cards.a: S-warfarin more albumin bound, so lower Vd

cards.q: Plasma volume effect on Vd of extensively bound drug
cards.a: Vd approaches plasma volume when no tissue binding

cards.q: Drugs with high Vd despite albumin binding
cards.a: Sequestered elsewhere in body

cards.q: Redistribution definition
cards.a: Drug moves from high-perfusion organs to muscle and fat as plasma level falls

cards.q: Why thiopentone action ends in minutes
cards.a: Redistribution away from brain

cards.q: Thiopental elimination half-life after single dose
cards.a: 3-8 hours; redistribution, not clearance, ends action

cards.q: Why oral diazepam gives 6-8 hour hypnotic action
cards.a: Redistribution, despite elimination half-life over 30 h

cards.q: Effect of repeated dosing on redistribution
cards.a: Low-perfusion sites fill; drug becomes longer acting

cards.q: What makes redistribution faster
cards.a: Greater lipid solubility

cards.q: Blood-brain barrier structure
cards.a: Endothelium with tight junctions, no large gaps, glial investment

cards.q: Blood-CSF barrier location
cards.a: Choroid plexus epithelium

cards.q: Which drugs enter CNS
cards.a: Only lipid-soluble drugs; streptomycin and neostigmine excluded

cards.q: Efflux transporters at BBB
cards.a: P-gp and OATP

cards.q: Enzymatic barrier at BBB: examples
cards.a: MAO and cholinesterase limit catecholamine, 5-HT and acetylcholine entry

cards.q: Sites where BBB is deficient
cards.a: Chemoreceptor trigger zone (medulla) and periventricular sites (anterior hypothalamus)

cards.q: What governs drug exit from CSF and brain
cards.a: CSF bulk flow via arachnoid villi, not lipid solubility

cards.q: Levodopa and dopamine: which enters the brain
cards.a: Levodopa enters; dopamine does not (used in parkinsonism)

cards.q: Condition that increases BBB permeability
cards.a: Inflamed meninges or brain

cards.q: Placental transfer: lipophilic versus hydrophilic drugs
cards.a: Lipophilic cross freely; hydrophilic restricted

cards.q: Is the placenta an absolute drug barrier?
cards.a: No; influx transporters exist and drugs reach the fetus

cards.q: Fetal plasma pH and effect on basic drugs
cards.a: About 7.0-7.2 versus maternal 7.4, so ion trapping of basic drugs

cards.q: Salicylate and fetal ion trapping
cards.a: Sodium salicylate undergoes ion trapping in the fetus

cards.q: Milk transfer of drugs: greatest when
cards.a: Low maternal protein binding and high lipid solubility

cards.q: Tissues where digoxin concentrates: list
cards.a: Skeletal muscle, heart, liver, kidney

cards.q: Tissues where chloroquine concentrates: list
cards.a: Liver, kidney, retina

cards.q: Tissues where tetracyclines concentrate: list
cards.a: Liver, bone and teeth

cards.q: Tissues where iodine concentrates
cards.a: Thyroid

cards.q: Tissue where ephedrine and atropine bind
cards.a: Iris, bound to melanin

cards.q: Tissue where thiopentone and ether concentrate
cards.a: Adipose tissue (dissolve in neutral fat)

cards.q: Tissue where bisphosphonates bind
cards.a: Bone (bound to hydroxyapatite)

cards.q: Brain concentrates: list
cards.a: Chlorpromazine, acetazolamide, isoniazid

cards.q: Local toxicity from tissue storage: tetracyclines
cards.a: Bone and teeth

cards.q: Local toxicity from tissue storage: chloroquine
cards.a: Retina

cards.q: Local toxicity from tissue storage: streptomycin
cards.a: Vestibular apparatus

cards.q: Local toxicity from tissue storage: emetine
cards.a: Heart and skeletal muscle

cards.q: Intracellular organelle binding: tetracycline and chloroquine
cards.a: Tetracycline to mitochondria; chloroquine to nuclei

cards.q: Poisons where haemodialysis is not useful (Better Care AVOID): list
cards.a: Benzodiazepines, chloroquine, amphetamine, verapamil, opioids, imipramine, digoxin

cards.q: Cloze: pH at which a weak acid is 50% ionised
cards.a: pKa
cards.text: At pH equal to pKa, a weak drug is 50% ionised.

cards.q: Cloze: energy in facilitated diffusion versus primary active transport
cards.a: No energy; ATP via ABC transporters
cards.text: Facilitated diffusion needs no energy; primary active transport uses ATP through ABC transporters.

cards.q: Cloze: gene encoding P-glycoprotein
cards.a: MDR1 (ABCB1)

cards.q: Cloze: formula for apparent volume of distribution
cards.a: Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration
cards.text: Apparent volume of distribution: Vd = amount of drug in body / plasma concentration.

cards.q: Cloze: why thiopentone action ends in minutes
cards.a: Redistribution from the brain
cards.text: Thiopentone action ends in minutes because of redistribution from the brain.

cards.q: Cloze: aspirin accumulation in gastric mucosal cells
cards.a: Ion trapping at pH 7.0
cards.text: Aspirin accumulates in gastric mucosal cells by ion trapping at pH 7.0.
